title: Distributed Unique ID Generator with NTP Clock Rollback Protection
subtitle: Twitter Snowflake Bit-Packing, Leap Seconds and Clock Backward Drift Mitigation
problem_statement: A distributed ID generator service produces 64-bit monotonically increasing identifiers across 32 nodes. During an NTP synchronization step-jump, the physical clock on node 14 rolls backward by 180 milliseconds. The service continues generating IDs, leading to duplicate primary keys and corrupted transactional ledgers.

faded_bug.description: Throwing an exception upon NTP clock rollback crashes the worker node rather than slewing or borrowing sequence tokens.

invariants.description: Zero duplicate IDs must be generated even during physical clock rollbacks.

probing_ladder.stage_1_validation: Explain the 64-bit layout of a Snowflake ID: timestamp bits, datacenter/worker bits, and sequence bits. Why is 4096 sequence numbers per millisecond sufficient?
probing_ladder.stage_2_tightening: During VM live migration in AWS/GCP, physical clocks can jump backwards by 200ms. If you spin-wait for 200ms on every thread, what happens to P99 latency and incoming TCP backlogs?
probing_ladder.stage_3_adversarial: Two worker nodes are accidentally assigned the same `worker_id` by Kubernetes during a split-brain deployment. How do you detect and prevent collision?
probing_ladder.stage_4_squeeze: Why not use UUIDv7 instead of maintaining a custom Snowflake cluster? Compare 128-bit index fragmentation in B-Trees with 64-bit Snowflake IDs.

counter_probes.counter_question: UUIDv4 is 128-bit and randomly distributed. What happens to database B-Tree index cache hit rate and page split frequency when inserting 1 billion rows with random UUIDs?
counter_probes.expected_staff_answer: Random UUIDs cause massive random I/O and B-Tree page splits because new rows do not append to the right edge. 64-bit monotonically increasing Snowflake IDs append sequentially with 99%+ page fill factor.
